strengths: Well-motivated problem: clinical need for CT reconstruction models that generalize across sampling rates and resolutions without retraining is clearly articulated and practically relevant.

Solid architectural design combining sinogram-space and image-space neural operators within an unrolled network, with a rotation-equivariant sinogram operator justified both theoretically (Appendix A) and via ablation.

Strong and consistent empirical gains over CNN, transformer (DuDoTrans, GloReDi), and diffusion (DPS, ALD) baselines across two datasets (Kidney CT, AAPM Abdomen) and multiple sparse-view settings (9/18/36/72 views), with clear PSNR/SSIM/RMSE improvements.
Practical advantage of ~500x faster inference than diffusion-based competitors while achieving better reconstruction quality, which is compelling for deployment.
Useful ablations isolating the contribution of rotational equivariance and of different frequency-domain learning configurations in the sinogram operator, supporting the design choices.

Zero-shot super-resolution experiments (both image-space and sinogram-space) demonstrate genuine resolution-agnostic behavior beyond the trained configurations, which is a meaningful validation of the core claim.
weaknesses: The core building blocks (DISCO convolutions, UDNO block) are adopted directly from prior work (Ocampo et al., Jatyani et al.), so the technical novelty largely lies in the CT-specific sinogram-domain formulation and rotation-equivariant padding scheme rather than a fundamentally new operator design; this should be more explicitly contextualized relative to the closely related MRI unified-model paper [22].

The 'resolution-agnostic across image resolutions' claim is validated mainly via zero-shot super-resolution rather than joint training across multiple output resolutions (unlike the sampling-rate experiments, which do use joint multi-rate training), making the cross-resolution generalization claim slightly weaker than the cross-sampling-rate claim.

Only two datasets are evaluated, both abdominal/kidney CT with similar geometry; broader validation (e.g., other anatomies, real clinical noise/artifact conditions, metal artifacts, limited-angle CT) would strengthen claims of general applicability.

The rotational-equivariance ablation shows a relatively modest improvement (0.83 dB), and it is unclear how much of the overall performance gain versus CNN baselines stems from this component versus the broader operator/dual-domain architecture.
No public code or data release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the architectural complexity (multiple UDNO branches, custom padding schemes, kernel basis hyperparameters).

Comparisons to other neural operator baselines (e.g., FNO-based CT models) are absent; only CNN, transformer, and diffusion baselines are considered, leaving open whether the specific DISCO/local-kernel choice is superior to alternative NO architectures for this task.
3D CT extension, which is clinically more relevant than 2D slices, is left as future work, somewhat limiting immediate real-world impact.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: sparse-view CT reconstruction models are typically tied to fixed sampling rates/resolutions, which is a genuine clinical limitation; the paper directly targets this gap with a neural-operator formulation.

Thoughtful architectural design: the sinogram-space operator is defined natively in polar (r,θ) coordinates with a principled rotation-equivariant padding scheme (grounded in the π-periodicity-with-flip identity), and the dual spatial/frequency branches are motivated by the Fourier slice theorem and classical FBP filtering, giving the design a clear theoretical grounding rather than being ad hoc.

Strong and consistent empirical gains across two datasets (Kidney C4KC-KiTS and AAPM abdominal) and multiple sampling rates (9/18/36/72 views), outperforming CNN baselines (~3-4dB), diffusion methods DPS/ALD (~3-6dB) with >500x inference speedup, and transformer/dual-domain baselines (DuDoTrans, GloReDi).

Genuine demonstration of resolution-agnostic behavior via zero-shot super-resolution experiments on both NOi (image-space, 256→512) and NOs (sinogram-space, 72→144 views) without retraining/fine-tuning, showing measurable gains over CNN counterparts with matched model size/receptive field ratio.
Useful ablations isolating the contribution of rotation-equivariant padding and the choice of frequency-domain transform axis, supporting the design decisions with quantitative evidence.

Clear writing and figures that effectively communicate the discretization problem and the proposed remedy, with reasonable implementation details (hyperparameters, training setup, baseline configurations) provided in the supplementary material to aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core building block (DISCO/UDNO) is adopted from prior work (Ocampo et al., Jatyani et al.); the paper's novelty is primarily in application-specific design (sinogram-domain operator, rotation equivariance, dual-branch frequency learning) rather than a new operator-learning technique, which somewhat limits the methodological contribution though the engineering and domain adaptation are non-trivial.

The rotation-equivariance ablation shows a relatively modest gain (0.83 dB at 24-view), raising a question about how much this specific design choice (versus the overall neural-operator/DISCO backbone) drives the headline improvements.

Evaluation is limited to two anatomically similar 2D CT datasets (kidney, abdomen); no 3D CT, no chest/other anatomies, and no evaluation on more extreme resolution or sampling-rate extrapolation (e.g., very low view counts, much higher resolutions than 512, or non-uniform/limited-angle sampling) that would more strongly stress-test the claimed resolution-agnostic generalization.

Some reported baselines show very high variance (e.g., GloReDi's PSNR std is nearly as large as CNN's mean gap), and no statistical significance testing is provided despite close margins for some comparisons (e.g., 36/72-view SSIM against DPS/ALD).

The zero-shot super-resolution experiments, while promising, are somewhat narrow in scope (single up-sampling factor tested for each of NOs and NOi) and would benefit from testing across a wider range of unseen resolutions/sampling rates to better substantiate the 'any resolution/any sampling rate' claim in the abstract.

No explicit statement on code/data release for reproducibility, despite detailed hyperparameters being given; this is a minor but relevant gap given reproducibility expectations for empirical contributions.

Limitations and failure-case discussion are minimal; the paper would benefit from analyzing scenarios where CTO underperforms (e.g., very sparse views, anatomical regions with fine structures) to give a fuller picture of the method's boundaries.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clinically relevant limitation of existing CT reconstruction networks — their inability to generalize across sampling rates and resolutions without retraining separate models — and is (to the authors' claim) the first application of neural operators to sparse-view CT.

Thorough empirical evaluation across two/three datasets (AAPM, Kidney/C4KC-KiTS, LIDC-IDRI in supplement), multiple sampling rates (9/18/36/72-view), and a wide range of baselines spanning learning-free, diffusion, single-pass, and unrolled-network categories.

Well-motivated architectural design: sinogram-domain operator in polar coordinates with joint spatial-frequency (Fourier-slice-theorem-inspired) processing, and rotation-equivariant circular padding with a formal derivation of the symmetry (Supp. A).

Strong and consistent empirical gains: >3.4dB PSNR over CNN baseline, ~3dB over diffusion SOTA with >500x faster inference, and clear zero-shot super-resolution benefits in both image and sinogram domains.

Extensive ablations (NOs/NOi component removal, rotational equivariance, frequency-transform axis choice, DISCO kernel hyperparameter sensitivity via Bayesian search, single-rate vs multi-rate training, OOD/noisy/cross-dataset generalization) that support the design choices and improve confidence in the results.
Careful complexity/runtime analysis showing DISCO-based operators match CNN inference cost while incurring only modest training-time overhead, addressing practical deployability concerns.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: DISCO convolutions and the U-shaped DISCO block are adopted largely unchanged from prior work (Liu-Schiaffini et al., Jatyani et al. for MRI); the main contribution is applying/adapting these established building blocks to a new domain (CT) with a dual-domain, polar-coordinate arrangement, rather than introducing a fundamentally new operator or theory.

All experiments use simulated sinograms generated from existing CT images via a forward Radon/fan-beam operator rather than real raw clinical acquisition data, which may not fully capture real scanner noise characteristics, detector nonlinearities, or other practical acquisition artifacts.
Only 2D reconstruction is studied; 3D CT (clinically standard for many protocols) is left to future work, limiting immediate clinical applicability despite motivating claims about clinical practice.

Baseline retraining under the multi-rate protocol departs from baselines' original single-rate designs, and some baseline numbers (e.g., DuDoTrans SSIM) appear much lower than in their original papers; while the authors flag this, it raises some concern about whether all baselines were optimally tuned for the multi-rate setting, potentially inflating the apparent margin of improvement.

The rotation-equivariance property is formally established only for the sinogram-space operator; it is not clearly shown (theoretically or empirically beyond qualitative visualization) that this equivariance is preserved through the image-space operator and data-consistency steps to yield exact end-to-end equivariance.

Zero-shot super-resolution across image resolutions relies on a bilinear upsampling step between the fixed-resolution sinogram operator and the higher-resolution image operator, which is a partly ad hoc bridge rather than a fully native cross-resolution operator design.
Limited discussion of failure modes, error bars/statistical significance testing between CTO and closest baselines, or qualitative analysis of when/why CTO underperforms, if at all.

strengths: First application of neural operators (DISCO-based) to sparse-view CT, addressing a well-motivated and clinically relevant problem: generalization of a single model across multiple sampling rates/resolutions without retraining.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two main datasets (AAPM, Kidney/C4KC-KiTS) plus an additional LIDC-IDRI dataset in the supplement, with a wide range of baselines spanning classical (FBP, SART), diffusion (DPS, ALD), transformer (RegFormer, DuDoTrans), and unrolled CNN methods.

Thoughtful architectural design choices grounded in CT physics: the sinogram-space operator in polar coordinates with spatial+frequency branches is motivated by the Fourier Slice Theorem and FBP, and the rotation-equivariant circular padding scheme is derived from the known π-periodicity-with-flip symmetry of parallel-beam sinograms.

Extensive ablation studies (NOs/NOi component removal, FFT-domain strategy comparison, DISCO hyperparameter sensitivity via Bayesian search, rotational equivariance effect, single-rate vs multi-rate training) that help isolate the source of gains.
Useful zero-shot super-resolution experiments in both sinogram and image domains that directly probe the core discretization-agnostic claim, going beyond simply reporting multi-rate PSNR tables.

Complexity/runtime analysis showing CTO's inference cost is essentially on par with CNNs (same FLOPs when kernel configuration matched) while being orders of magnitude faster than diffusion-based reconstruction, with supporting FLOP/parameter breakdowns.
Additional robustness experiments addressing noisy sinograms and cross-dataset transfer, which strengthen the practical relevance of the claims beyond clean, in-distribution settings.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a recombination of existing building blocks (DISCO convolutions and UDNO blocks from prior MRI/PDE neural-operator work, unrolled network design from MoDL) applied to a new domain, rather than a fundamentally new operator or theoretical advance; the novelty claims (e.g., 'first NO framework for CT') should be read as domain-transfer novelty rather than methodological novelty.

The diffusion baseline (DPS/ALD) appears to be trained for only 2,000 iterations, which is unusually short for diffusion models and raises concerns that the reported '500x faster, 3dB better' comparison against diffusion may not reflect a well-trained/tuned diffusion baseline; more detail on diffusion training convergence (loss curves, comparison to published diffusion CT baselines) would strengthen the claim.

All baselines are retrained under a 'multi-rate' protocol that differs from their original published training regime; while the paper argues this is for fairness, it is unclear whether baseline architectures (e.g., RegFormer, LEARN) were adequately re-tuned (learning rate, capacity, number of iterations) to perform optimally under this new regime, potentially understating baseline performance and inflating relative gains.

Resolution-agnosticism is demonstrated mainly via a single doubling of resolution and view count (zero-shot 2x super-resolution); the claims of general discretization-agnostic behavior across arbitrarily different scanner geometries, detector spacings, and anatomical scales are not stress-tested (e.g., no experiments at very different resolutions, non-square grids, or substantially different detector counts beyond the two tested settings).

The rotation-equivariance property is demonstrated only for simple global object rotations (0°, 90°, 180°) in simulated parallel/fan-beam geometry; real clinical CT involves gantry tilt, non-ideal beam geometries, and patient motion, so the practical benefit of this property in realistic acquisition settings is not established.

All experiments use simulated sparse-view sinograms derived from fully-sampled CT images rather than real sparse-view acquisitions or physical phantom data, limiting evidence for clinical applicability despite framing the motivation around clinical deployment.

No uncertainty quantification or calibration analysis is provided, which is particularly relevant for a clinical imaging application where confidence in reconstructed structures matters; this is acknowledged only as future work.

The DISCO-vs-CNN complexity analysis shows a non-trivial 20-42% FLOP overhead during training, and the full CTO model incurs ~1.3x FLOPs and ~1.1x parameters over the matched-capacity CNN ablation, which somewhat tempers the 'resolution-agnostic at no extra inference cost' narrative, even though inference-time parity is demonstrated.

The single-rate vs. multi-rate ablation central to motivating the paper's framing (Table 2a) only includes two competing baselines (LEARN, RegFormer), a relatively narrow basis for the broad claim that 'existing methods overfit to a fixed acquisition setup.'

strengths: First application of neural operators (via DISCO discrete-continuous convolutions) to sparse-view CT reconstruction, directly addressing a well-motivated and practically important limitation of existing CNN/transformer-based methods (rigid tie to fixed sampling rate/resolution).

The dual-domain architecture is well-justified physically: the sinogram-space operator NOs, defined in polar (r, θ) coordinates with a spatial+frequency dual-branch design, is explicitly connected to the Fourier slice theorem and to FBP's ramp-filter intuition, giving the design a principled rather than purely empirical motivation.

The rotation-equivariant convolution design (flipped circular padding respecting the π-periodicity-with-flip identity of parallel-beam sinograms) is a genuinely CT-specific architectural contribution, with both a formal derivation (Supp. A) and empirical validation (qualitative rotation consistency, +0.83dB ablation).

Extensive and fairly rigorous experimental evaluation: two primary datasets (AAPM, Kidney) plus a third (LIDC-IDRI) in supplementary, multiple sampling rates (9/18/36/72-view), many strong and diverse baselines (learning-free, diffusion DPS/ALD, transformer/dual-domain single-pass methods, unrolled networks), consistent multi-rate training protocol applied fairly across all methods.

Strong and consistent empirical gains (~3-6dB PSNR over CNN/diffusion/transformer baselines) alongside a substantial (>500x) inference speed advantage over diffusion-based SOTA, which is a compelling practicality argument.

Thorough ablation and analysis suite: NOs/NOi component ablations, frequency-branch design sweep (Supp Fig. 6c), Bayesian hyperparameter search over DISCO kernel configuration with importance/correlation analysis, OOD tests (Poisson noise, cross-dataset transfer), and a careful complexity analysis showing DISCO does not add inference-time overhead versus a matched CNN.
Zero-shot super-resolution experiments in both image and sinogram space (Sec 5.3) provide meaningful evidence for the core resolution-agnostic claim beyond the primary multi-rate results.
weaknesses: The core building blocks (DISCO convolutions, UDNO block) are adopted essentially unchanged from prior neural-operator literature (Liu-Schiaffini et al. for DISCO, Jatyani et al. for UDNO in MRI); the paper's novelty is primarily in adapting/combining these components for the CT sinogram-image dual-domain setting rather than introducing fundamentally new operator theory, which somewhat tempers the claimed originality.

All experiments are restricted to 2D reconstruction on 256x256 (or similar) grids; 3D CT, which is standard in most clinical workflows, is deferred entirely to future work, limiting the immediate clinical relevance of the claims made in the introduction.

Resolution-agnosticism is demonstrated mainly through zero-shot super-resolution at a single fixed factor (256->512) and through varying view counts; broader resolution ranges, non-integer scale factors, or more diverse detector geometries are not explored, leaving the generality of the "resolution-agnostic" claim only partially substantiated.

Evaluation relies solely on standard image-quality metrics (RMSE/PSNR/SSIM) without any clinical/diagnostic-task-based validation (e.g., lesion detectability, radiologist review), despite the paper's repeated emphasis on clinical applicability and organ/protocol variability as motivation.

The efficiency comparison against diffusion methods, while impressive, primarily reflects the well-known general speed disadvantage of iterative diffusion posterior sampling rather than a property unique to the proposed neural-operator design; a comparison with faster single-step or distilled diffusion variants would give a more complete picture.

Noise robustness is tested only for a single Poisson noise level (I0=10^6), and cross-dataset OOD evaluation is limited to one transfer direction (Kidney->AAPM), so the breadth of OOD/robustness claims is somewhat narrow relative to how strongly they are emphasized in the text.
